description: Human Orchestra is made up of Software Engineering students from UABC in Baja California, Mexico. We bring together full-stack development, data handling, and a hands-on, collaborative mindset. Our goal is to turn NASA’s open data and challenges into innovative solutions, and to grow as engineers while doing it.
summary:
Imagine landing a spacecraft at the Moon’s south pole. The Sun there never climbs more than a few degrees above the horizon, so a ridge can block it and leave your lander without power. The same terrain can hide the Earth and cut your radio link home. Land in the wrong place or on the wrong day, and the mission can end in the dark.

LuNAV shows that risk before anyone takes it. It combines NASA’s terrain data with the real positions of the Sun and the Earth, checked against JPL Horizons, to work out when each site has sunlight and a line of sight to Earth. Planners compare sites and arrival days side by side to find the best window. Then they fly the chosen plan in 3D, from launch to landing, and stand under the site’s real sky.

At Haworth, one of NASA’s candidate regions, arriving one day later stretches the longest night of a week-long stay from 10 hours to 34, long enough to drain the battery of our simulated lander. LuNAV makes this visible to mission planners, teachers and anyone who has wondered what it takes to survive a night at the Moon’s south pole.
details:
What it does

LuNAV helps mission planners, educators and the public choose where and when to land at the lunar south pole. A mission plan is a landing site, an arrival date and a stay of 3, 7 or 14 days. For each plan the app gives the share of time in sunlight, the longest night, the minimum and mean hours per day with Earth in view, and the longest communication gap. It also gives a combined score that weights sunlight at 40%, short nights at 30% and Earth contact at 30%.

The app has four parts.

  • Mission Planner. You pick one of five sites on a map of the south pole shaded by NASA’s average-illumination data, then an arrival date and a stay. The site panel explains the plan in plain language. It also compares the plan with the days around it and with the other sites on the same day. “Find the best plan” searches every precomputed plan for that stay length (5 sites × 365 arrival days). You set a minimum sunlight, a maximum darkness and a minimum daily Earth contact. Use the sliders, or type the limits in plain English, for example “at least 80% sunlight and no more than 24 hours of darkness”. You can also click any point from 85°S to the pole, or type its coordinates, and analyze that spot instead.
  • Search and compare. You pin 2 to 5 plans and see them side by side in identical 2D panels. Each panel has the terrain horizon with the Sun and Earth tracks, a time ribbon of light and Earth link, and the main metrics. One shared time slider moves every panel at once.
  • Launch and Land. Only the chosen plan opens in 3D, with the Earth, Moon and Sun at their real positions for that date. An illustrative mission launches at local noon from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center and reaches a 200 km parking orbit. It spends about three days in transfer, is captured into a low lunar orbit and makes a powered descent while the camera follows it down to the site. On the surface you see the real LOLA terrain with shadows, the Sun and Earth in the sky, and a 360° horizon panorama. A countdown gives the time left until the next sunset and Earthset and says what happens next. The Sky view shows the 3D scene full screen, and the Data view shows the 2D charts.
  • Educator. The mission is told in four short chapters and ends with the challenge “Can your lander make it?”. The player picks any point and an arrival day. The app then shows right away whether an assumed lander keeps its power for the whole stay, and why.

How it works

An offline Python pipeline computes everything in advance with one command. The browser only filters and draws the results, so LuNAV needs no server and runs as a static site on GitHub Pages.

  1. The five sites are in five USGS Artemis III candidate regions: Connecting Ridge, Haworth, Nobile Rim 1, Malapert Massif and de Gerlache Rim 2. In each region we take the highest point of the LOLA elevation model inside the official polygon. It is a representative point, not the planned site of any mission.
  2. To get each site’s horizon, we trace rays across the LRO LOLA 40 m/pixel south polar elevation model. We use 360 one-degree azimuth bins, go out to 100 km and correct for lunar curvature. The observer stands 3 m above the ground.
  3. NASA/JPL SPICE kernels (DE440, MOON_ME frame, light-time and stellar aberration corrections) give the Sun and Earth positions every 30 minutes for all of 2027.
  4. The Sun counts as up when its upper edge clears the terrain. A direct Earth link needs the center of the Earth to be 0.5° above the terrain, as an antenna margin.
  5. The pipeline computes the metrics for all 5,475 plans, and a shared data contract checks the output in both Python and TypeScript.

For custom coordinates, the browser does the work itself from precomputed SPICE vectors and a reduced version of the LOLA relief. The app marks these results APPROXIMATE: their horizon differs from the full 40 m masks by 0.16° to 0.25° on average.

Validation

  • Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation match JPL Horizons. Across 70 comparisons the worst difference is 0.0016″, against a tolerance of 0.05°. The same test catches a deliberately wrong reference frame, which is off by 101.6″.
  • The Moon’s phase in the 3D scene is within 0.134 percentage points of Horizons, and the 3D sky agrees with the 2D data within 0.031°.
  • A permanently shadowed point on the floor of Shackleton crater gets 0.00% sunlight. The five sites get between 71% and 95% over the year.
  • Parity tests show that the browser code reproduces all 5,475 plans published by the Python pipeline.

Benefits and intended impact

Tools that compute Sun and Earth positions for candidate sites already exist, but their interfaces make it slow to compare sites and dates. In LuNAV a planner changes a date or a site and sees the result at once. The planner can find the risky nights and back a choice with numbers.

Timing matters a lot. At Haworth, a 7-day stay that starts on 10 January 2027 gets 94.1% sunlight and its longest night lasts 10 h. Starting one day later gives 79.8% sunlight and a 34 h night, long enough to leave an assumed lander battery empty for 14.5 h.

For educators and the public, the 3D sky makes the problem visible: the Sun never rises more than a few degrees, and the Earth stays close to the horizon.

The code is open source under the MIT License. Dependency versions are pinned and every data file has a recorded checksum, so anyone can rerun the pipeline and get the same data. Hosting the site costs nothing.

What makes it creative

Our design rule is “2D to compare, 3D to understand”. Plans are compared in simple 2D panels that never use WebGL, and only the chosen plan opens in 3D. The 3D part is one continuous journey, from the launch pad in Florida to standing on the site and watching the Sun move along the horizon. The Educator challenge turns the same data into a game. The rocket is a procedural model built in code, and the ambient music and mission-control sounds are synthesized live with the Web Audio API. Constraints can also be typed in plain English.

Tools and technologies

  • Data pipeline: Python 3.13, SpiceyPy, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, pandas, pydantic, Matplotlib, Pillow and pytest.
  • Front end: React 19 with TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, three.js, Zod, Vitest and the Web Audio API.
  • Data: NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440); JPL Horizons; the LRO LOLA south polar elevation model (NASA GSFC PGDA, Barker et al. 2023); LOLA average polar illumination (Mazarico et al. 2011); USGS Artemis III candidate regions (McClernan 2024); the IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature; NASA SVS textures of the Moon and Earth.
  • Infrastructure: Git, GitHub, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages, plus Puppeteer scripts for performance and screenshot checks.
  • Hardware: only ordinary laptops. The 3D scene runs at 60 fps on integrated Intel Iris Xe graphics.
  • AI assistance: we used Claude Code (Anthropic) as a coding assistant under written project rules. The rules say never invent scientific data, label anything simulated, and check every result with tests and JPL Horizons.

Factors we considered

We were strict about scientific honesty. The interface labels every simplification: trajectories are ILLUSTRATIVE, custom-coordinate terrain is APPROXIMATE, and the lander battery is ASSUMED (5,000 Wh, 250 W load, 750 W of panels). Nothing synthetic is shown as real.

Terrain drives every metric, because a tool that plots ephemerides without terrain gives wrong answers at the south pole.

For performance, the app keeps a single WebGL context and the 2D panels never use WebGL. The 3D scene holds 60 fps and five comparison panels redraw in about 7 ms. The data load progressively, with a total under 50 MB.

For accessibility, everything works with the keyboard, there is a reduced-motion mode, and information is shown by shape as well as color. Every value has a tooltip and a screen-reader description with its method and source.

We designed for three audiences: precise numbers for planners, a narrated story for educators and an immersive sky for the public. All data sources are credited in the app and in the README.

GitHub Repository Link: https://github.com/luismar-ing/LuNAV.git
